sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner screens before filing, and the screen starts with three qualifying buckets. Adam Cartabiano lays them out on the Ryan Downs show: a fully out-of-network event where the admit source was the emergency room, an out-of-network charge on an in-network event, and emergency air ambulance [0BGnlP4Q71M @ 00:00:23]. Cartabiano flags a common misperception. The rule is not limited to ED patients; it turns on admit source. A patient who came through the ED and matriculated to observation or inpatient status still qualifies, and inpatient is where the big dollars come into play [0BGnlP4Q71M @ 00:00:40]. The second bucket drives most of the volume in the public CMS files: anesthesiologists, ED docs, hospitalists, pathologists, radiologists and surgical groups. Team Health and SCP are named as the biggest private submitters [0BGnlP4Q71M @ 00:01:32]. K&L Gates partner Steve Pine maps the same perimeter from the statute side. It covers emergency services at an out-of-network facility including facility fees, emergency and non-emergency services by out-of-network providers inside in-network facilities, and out-of-network air ambulance. Ground ambulance is excluded [VbqFYBvnpas @ 00:01:30]. CMS presenter Amanda Brander repeats the identical three triggers as step one of the pre-IDR sequence [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:03:30].

The second consensus point is that plan funding decides the route, and getting it wrong ends the claim. Cartabiano splits the map into two kinds of states. Federal states push everything through the CMS process. In bifurcated states, fully funded plans governed by the state Department of Insurance go to the state process, while ERISA self-insured populations still follow the federal track [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:00:20]. The instruction is blunt: read the insurance card or call the payer to confirm self-insured versus fully funded, because you'll get kicked out if you send it to the wrong place [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:01:25]. Andres, CBO at Lido, has codified this fork in Lido's eligibility audit engine. A fully insured Texas plan goes to SB 1264 arbitration, and self-funded ERISA plans go federal. The team calls the full rule set quite complicated, which is why they hard-coded it [NHWPEtUOyK0 @ 00:04:44]. Brander adds the detail that keeps volume federal. Some states let self-funded plans opt into the state process, but nothing forces them to. The federal process stays open to every self-insured plan that has not opted in, and to FEHB carriers whose Office of Personnel Management contract does not direct them to a state process [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:17:56]. Plan type is therefore the first field verified, not the last.

Third, nobody skips open negotiation and nobody files everything. Brander sets the clock: open negotiation must be initiated within 30 business days, starting the day the provider receives the initial payment or denial notice. Both sides must participate in good faith and hand over the information needed if talks fail [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:05:08]. Cartabiano explains why the step is non-optional in practice. You must show proof you went through it, and if you skip it the arbitration organization rejects the claim. A payer that simply ignores you does not owe the demand; you just advance to arbitration [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:02:51]. On selection, Lido's Andres opens the Lido workflow with a two-part filter. Is the claim NSA eligible? Even if it is, is the expected award value worth the IDR route [NHWPEtUOyK0 @ 00:00:51]? Vee Healthtek turns that filter into a triage grid. Every paid out-of-network account goes into one of four bins: payment complete, recovery justified, value undetermined, or likely recovery that does not justify the cost. Each bin gets its own action: close accurate accounts, prioritize supported recovery, correct missing data before estimating the gap, and monitor low-value patterns without chasing every balance [GpHExH5dquQ @ 00:00:32].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The execution clock runs in fixed blocks. The open negotiation notice must carry dates of service, service codes, the initial payment or denial notice, an out-of-network rate offer, and sender contact details. Brander relays a payer-side complaint that the form cannot identify the customer. Providers solve it by adding their own fields or attaching an EOB; otherwise the payer reaches back for information [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:09:52]. Cartabiano anchors that offer to the in-network commercial equivalent. Audits of client organizations find a 50/50 split. The half paid around 15 to 17 percent of billed charges, against a QPA typically couched at roughly 100 to 115 percent of Medicare, is the population targeted toward 45, 50, or 55 percent of charges [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:03:38]. When the 30 business days expire without a deal, the CMS web form demo allows four business days to initiate [cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:00:05]. Staffingly calls that window absolute: a miss forfeits the claim entirely [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:02:49]. Cartabiano explains why four days hurts. The arbitration package is far heavier than the single negotiation letter, and fresh claims keep rolling off their own negotiation periods while the team builds it. Without structure, the workload compounds fast.

Inside the Notice of IDR Initiation web form, the traps are mechanical. The demo warns the form must be completed in one session and times out after 60 minutes of inactivity. An open negotiation start date more than 34 business days back triggers an extension-justification prompt, and at least one upload proving that start date is mandatory [cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:04:22]. Each line item needs a claim number, date of service, QPA, a claim-and-QPA document, cost sharing, service code, up to four two-character modifiers, and place of service. The portal blocks any duplicate combination of claim number, date, code, and modifier unless a cooling-off closure or approved extension applies [cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:11:17]. CMS's Matt Meidell fixes the offer math. The offer is the full amount requested, including what was already paid, expressed both as a dollar figure and as a percentage of the QPA. The QPA entered should match the initial payment or denial notice [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:20:34]. Lido's Andres flags the newest bottleneck: the centralized IDR gateway no longer offers an API. Filers either key data manually or use a vendor that automates entry without one, which Lido claims to have caught ahead of the market [NHWPEtUOyK0 @ 00:06:21].

Batching is where fee savings and rejections collide. Meidell lists the four batching tests: same provider, group, or facility; same plan or issuer; same or similar service code; and all items furnished within the same 30 business day period [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:23:43]. Staffingly confirms CMS allows grouping to save fees but says improperly grouped claims are immediately rejected [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:02:33]. The evidence package is the other heavy lift. Cartabiano's three core elements are a demographic case positioning the organization as one that commands premium in-network rates, a clinical complexity review pulled from the medical record, and a financial comparison. That comparison lines up the in-network commercial rate, amount paid, Medicare, and Medicaid for that service and region, with specifics rather than broad strokes [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:05:47]. Cartabiano sharpens the package by meeting IDR entities directly to learn what they score as a successful argument, then building that feedback into the process. The CoGenetix and ANS Solutions team builds the same thing as standing provider profiles covering credentials, service complexity, and regional market benchmarks. They argue fellowship training and surgical complexity are powerful arbitration tools for orthopedic groups [dTrA6r3pGyE @ 00:01:54].

callout.title: Filing-floor moves that protect the claim and the margin
callout.body: Four tactics practitioners use to keep offers alive, rank inventory, and sharpen submissions before the four-day window closes.
items: Pay the IDR entity fee and the administrative fee together with the offer. An offer is not considered received until both are paid, and an unreceived offer hands the other side its number as the final payment amount [CMSHHSgov — 7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:25:17]

Rank inventory by net recoverable value, not balance size. Weigh the likely additional payment, filing expense, specialist effort, and time remaining, and keep evidence preparation upstream of the filing decision [Vee Healthtek — s3194z7bdwY @ 00:00:54]

Aggregate small variances. A $200 recoverable gap across 5,000 claims equals $1 million before fees and collection costs, so per-claim thresholds should not hide recurring exposure [Vee Healthtek — GpHExH5dquQ @ 00:01:25]
Meet with the IDR entities and ask what they treat as a successful argument. They will tell you, and that feedback goes straight back into the submission process [Ryan Downs — 7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:09:44]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Win-rate math is where the vendor pitches split hardest. CoGenetix and ANS Solutions open with a win rate of over 90% for providers, later quoting a 90% to 95% track record, and cite industry data showing approximately 86% of decisions favoring providers [dTrA6r3pGyE @ 00:01:16]. Staffingly runs a lower headline of 88% wins with payouts averaging 450% of the qualifying payment amount, then immediately cuts that number down: one in five disputes was deemed ineligible due to errors and yielded zero recovery [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:01:25]. Adam Cartabiano, appearing on Ryan Downs' mini episodes, attacks the idea that any win rate is predictable at the claim level. He says IDREs lack an objective way to evaluate each claim on its own merit, so two identical claims for the same service, submitted with identical information, can split with one won and one lost [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:09:05]. Some IDREs judge holistically from a case-rate perspective while others go through every single CPT, HCPCS and DRG code before landing on a fair number [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:08:28]. His fix is consistency: meet with the IDREs to learn what they treat as a successful argument, then build that feedback into purpose-built technology so every submission argues the same way with high confidence.

The fee-risk story depends entirely on who is talking. CoGenetix tells providers that IDR filing fees are a necessary component but are typically reimbursed by the payer because the win rate is so high, framing the whole program as a low-risk, high-reward strategy [dTrA6r3pGyE @ 00:02:11]. Staffingly paints the opposite picture at system scale, citing Georgetown University research that IDR administrative fees reached $844 million in just the first half of 2025, and argues that practices managing the workflow internally are actively losing money once labor costs and filing-error penalties are counted [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:00:49]. CMS staff on the disputing-party call draw the hard line: administrative fees are non-refundable, although they should not be collected until the certified IDR entity finishes its initial screening for eligibility [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:26:12]. Vee Healthtek runs a middle playbook built on pre-filing triage. It ranks inventory by net recoverable value, weighing likely additional payment, filing expense, specialist effort and time remaining, and warns that a large balance is not automatically the best opportunity when stronger evidence and cheaper collection sit elsewhere [s3194z7bdwY @ 00:01:11]. A repeated payer methodology hitting hundreds of similar claims, in its view, calls for negotiation, payment validation or an upstream correction instead of recovering the same shortfall dispute after dispute.

Operating models diverge on who carries the workload. Staffingly prices an in-house specialist at $55,000 to $75,000 a year against 32% annual billing turnover and an average 68 days to replace, then sells an outsourced, AI-augmented team for a flat $399 per week, with most practices live in 14 days [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:04:27]. CoGenetix goes strictly performance-based, with no upfront costs and a tiered structure, plus a complimentary out-of-network assessment to open the relationship [dTrA6r3pGyE @ 00:03:49]. Lido splits the difference, running an end-to-end IDR resolution service internally while letting customers who prefer to do the process themselves work the same eligibility data in its portal. Even the IDRE selection mechanics get described differently. Cartabiano says there are 13 IDRE vendors, soon going to 15, and that the payer can reject the provider's pick up to three times before the fourth gets assigned automatically [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:07:36]. CMS staff describe a tighter clock: the non-initiating party has three business days to agree with the preferred entity or make an alternative selection, and if the parties cannot agree, the Departments randomly select a certified IDR entity no later than six business days after initiation and notify both sides by email [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:16:43].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures happen on the clock, not in front of the arbitrator. Staffingly calls the post-negotiation filing slot an absolute four business day window and says missing it forfeits the claim entirely [ASHyX7v13Eo @ 00:02:49]. Cartabiano explains why teams blow it: the open negotiation letter is one form with a small amount of information, but the arbitration submission needs hospital demographic positioning, a clinical complexity review pulled from the medical record, and a financial comparison of in-network commercial, paid, Medicare and Medicaid rates, all while new cases keep running off their own negotiation periods [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:05:47]. Skipping open negotiation is fatal too, because the arbitration organization rejects the claim without proof that the first step happened [7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:02:51]. Venue mistakes kill files before the clock even matters. In bifurcated states, fully funded plans governed by the state Department of Insurance go to the state process while self-insured ERISA populations stay federal, and Cartabiano warns that sending a claim to the wrong place gets it kicked out. Lido codifies the same split, routing fully insured Texas plans to SB 1264 arbitration and self-funded ERISA plans to federal IDR [NHWPEtUOyK0 @ 00:04:44].

The CMS web form demos surface a second layer of traps that cost operators real filings. The Notice of IDR Initiation form must be completed in a single session and times out after 60 minutes of inactivity; it requires at least one upload proving the open negotiation start date, and if that date is more than 34 business days before the current date it forces an extension justification [cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:04:22]. Answering that the provider received patient consent to waive surprise billing protections makes the dispute ineligible, and the form blocks duplicate line items sharing the same claim number, date of service, service code and modifiers [cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:11:17]. After submission the burden flips to the filer: CMS staff say the initiation notice will not be available in the portal, so the initiating party must send the copy to the non-initiating party directly [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:15:33]. On the resubmission form, the filer must hit Print PDF before Continue Submitting because there is no way back to that confirmation page afterwards, and the initiating party alone is responsible for confirming every regrouped line item still meets batching and bundling criteria [Vy31vkzfNBE @ 00:09:48]. The original demo adds that the PDF copy goes to the non-initiating party on the same day the form is submitted.

Economics checks fail quietly upstream. Vee Healthtek warns that a paid out-of-network claim can still leave recoverable money behind because payment status confirms that money moved, not that the amount was accurate; automatic adjustments hide variances before a specialist ever looks, and a $200 recoverable variance across 5,000 claims is $1 million before fees and collection costs [GpHExH5dquQ @ 00:01:25]. Its second video adds that recovery can fail before arbitration begins when a low payment posts as final and the opportunity closes before anyone takes responsibility [s3194z7bdwY @ 00:00:00]. Lido shows the document version of that failure: a missing 835 and EOB block a final eligibility call even when the CMS-1500 lines up with the NSA rules [NHWPEtUOyK0 @ 00:02:50]. Inside the process, CMS staff spell out a default trap: an offer is not considered received until both the certified IDR entity fee and the administrative fee are paid, and if one side's offer is not received the entity selects the other party's offer as the final payment amount [7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:25:17]. They also want the offer stated as the full requested amount including anything already paid, expressed as a dollar figure and a percentage of the QPA, and the QPA entered should be the one listed on the initial payment or denial notice.

callout.title: Pre-Filing Kill Switches
callout.body: Run every claim through these four checks before a dollar of fees or an hour of specialist time goes into an IDR filing.
items: Confirm plan funding and state route first, because a claim sent to the wrong process gets kicked out [Ryan Downs — 7lqb5ev54mA @ 00:01:25].

Hold any initiation that lacks an uploaded proof of the open negotiation start date, and expect an extension justification if that date is more than 34 business days old [CMSHHSgov — cw4MI_h6Gns @ 00:04:22].
Never let a posted remit close the account; one owner carries the claim position, deadline and unresolved barriers [Vee Healthtek — s3194z7bdwY @ 00:00:17].
Pay both the certified IDR entity fee and the administrative fee with the offer, or the other side's offer wins by default [CMSHHSgov — 7lzQt8aAlG0 @ 00:25:17].

chapters.question_prompt: How are the IDR Operations Final Rule, court rulings, and pending legislation changing access, batching, fees, and timing for disputing parties?
chapters.title: The Shifting Rulebook: IDR Operations Final Rule, TMA Litigation, and Congressional Fixes
chapters.subtitle: New federal IDR portal, batching limits, administrative and entity fees, November 1, 2026 deadline changes for radiology, TMA III ruling impacts, Pallone and Cassidy proposals, payer and TPA reality checks, and competing reform agendas from Georgetown CHIR, Paragon, and hospital coalitions
chapters.executive_summary: Payer, provider, and policy practitioners agree that the No Surprises Act's patient protections work. IDR is where the system broke: 17,000 expected disputes became more than 2.6 million, a handful of repeat filers including HaloMD drive most of the volume, and providers win roughly 85 to 88 percent of determinations. The May 28, 2026 operations final rule changes the plumbing, not the substance. The CMS administrative fee drops from $115 to $15 per party. Batches are capped at 50 line items for open negotiations starting on or after November 1, 2026. Non-initiating parties must respond by business day 15. A 30-business-day cooling-off period now feeds a four-business-day filing window with no grace period, and unregistered plans default at the offer stage. Practitioners split on whether the batch cap rose from 25 or from unlimited, and on whether the rule fixes anything that matters.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus: Protections Work, IDR Broke, and the Rulebook Keeps Moving
paragraphs: Across payer, provider, and policy camps, the starting point is the same: the patient-protection half of the No Surprises Act works, and the arbitration half is where the money leaks. Brian O'Hara of The Phia Group says the law 'really did accomplish its goal of preventing surprise balance bills' and argues that reform should not weaken those protections [8QIP4F1EGTA @ 00:01:47]. The volume numbers explain why IDR became the battlefield for every stakeholder. Kenna Watts at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms puts 2025 IDR costs above $16 billion, roughly 3.5 times the prior year. The expectation was 17,000 disputes; the actual count was more than 2.6 million, or upward of 7,000 a day [wJkWOgxZj6k @ 00:10:12]. Paragon's panel lands in the same zone with different counting: a 22,000-per-year estimate versus 258,000 merit line items in 2023 and 4.2 million in 2025, about 5.7 million counting every dispute [PpfXacIXrAc @ 00:11:31]. O'Hara adds the business-model read: a few provider groups have turned IDR into routine revenue-cycle management rather than an exception process [8QIP4F1EGTA @ 00:05:07]. The numbers disagree on scale, but nobody on either side argues that the original forecast survived contact with the market. That volume is the baseline every workflow change now has to absorb.

The second point of consensus is that a small set of repeat filers drives the machine and wins most of the time. Watts reports that five provider groups file roughly three-quarters of all disputes: four private-equity staffing groups plus HaloMD. The staffing groups win 90 to 96 percent, awards run 6 to 10 times the median in-network rate, and up to $1.4 billion has gone to contingency fees [wJkWOgxZj6k @ 00:12:03]. HaloMD does not dodge its footprint. Its own leadership says the firm initiates about 22 percent of IDR disputes and operates in all 50 states [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:00:32]. Brady Bazar of The Phia Group, working from CMS data for January to June 2025, puts provider wins at about 88 percent of determinations and plan wins at 12 percent. The prevailing offer landed above the QPA in about 88 percent of cases [ksxW878eWWk @ 00:07:44]. Paragon tracks the trend line: provider win rates of 82.1 percent in 2023 and 85.2 percent in 2025. In Major League Baseball arbitration, the format members believed would force reasonable offers, players win 45 percent and owners 55 percent [PpfXacIXrAc @ 00:12:43]. Whichever dataset an operator trusts, the payer side loses the large majority of determinations, and the filers on the other side are concentrated and still growing every year.

The third point of consensus is that the rulebook keeps shifting and the newest federal rule changes the plumbing, not the substance. KLGates describes the final rule issued May 28, 2026 by HHS, Labor, Treasury, and OPM as operational rather than substantive. It was driven by the hundreds of thousands of claims filed since 2022, far more than the agencies anticipated [NwapzBNojY0 @ 00:00:39]. Katie Johnson of the American Benefits Council calls the rules an 'initial step' that took years to finalize. Johnson says substantial further improvement and oversight are needed and that the rules miss 'the most egregious areas of abuse' [30BDiubQ0cg @ 00:00:59]. Underneath the rule, the courts keep rewriting the math. The Zelis speaker puts it bluntly: 'litigation continues to kind of steer the policy.' TMA3 on QPA calculation is unresolved, and CMS typically follows major rulings with guidance 6 to 12 months later [D63N2KsthY8 @ 00:05:52]. Ron Howrigan of Fulcrum Strategies reports that Judge Kernodle sided with TMA on every QPA calculation point and vacated the guidance. TMA lost on disclosure because the statute is not prescriptive there, which leaves CMS deference, and Howrigan scores the outcome a 'triple' [f9Q5ImwNeS0 @ 00:09:18]. Any team running eligibility, QPA, or payment workflows is working against a target that moves with each ruling and each guidance cycle.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers: Fees, Batches, Clocks, and the Registry
paragraphs: The headline mechanic is the cost of entry, and every camp quotes the same number. HaloMD's team states that the CMS non-refundable administrative fee 'is going from $115 to $15' per party, $30 total for both sides, effective June 11, 2026 [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:02:33]. Anders Gilberg of MGMA, whose group advocated for the cut, calls it 'a significant reduction' and says that 'for smaller practices that is a huge improvement' [K4eVTdf3xa0 @ 00:04:28]. Xpert Billing Talk supplies the street math behind that statement: a $150 anesthesia claim was not worth fighting at $115, because 'you'd basically lose money trying to get your money' [CwSXrQBZiOg @ 00:02:01]. Batching is the second lever, and its trigger is a date rather than a dollar figure. According to Xpert's radiology briefing, open negotiations starting on or after November 1, 2026 are 'strictly capped at exactly 50 line items, period.' Those batched disputes then sit through a new 30-business-day cooling-off period meant to force negotiation and clear the backlog, while single, bundled, and older batch disputes keep the 90-calendar-day rules [g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:00:45]. The operating consequence Xpert spells out is two parallel tracking systems running at once: one for legacy disputes and one keyed to the open-negotiation start date of every new batched dispute in the queue.

The clocks are where cases now die. KLGates reports that the final rule requires the non-initiating party, 'which is often the payer, to issue a response by the 15th business day of the open negotiation period,' inside the 30-business-day window [NwapzBNojY0 @ 00:04:19]. HaloMD adds the fine print: that response requires no counteroffer, and the non-initiating party must answer an IDR initiation within 3 business days [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:10:39]. The batch side is less forgiving. Once the cooling-off period ends, Xpert describes a four-business-day filing window that the portal enforces with no grace period. Late claims 'just get dumped right into your denial management queues as permanent losses,' and Xpert says spreadsheets are inadequate for tracking the window [g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:02:21]. On the back end, The Phia Group reminds plans that 'the IDR awards have to be paid within 30 calendar days of the date that a determination is rendered' and tells them to build a dedicated award-payment tracker [ksxW878eWWk @ 00:14:13]. Each of these deadlines is counted differently: business days on the negotiation and filing side, calendar days on the payment side. That is why Xpert pushes a calendar-based tool and Phia pushes a standalone tracker for every determination that lands against a plan.

The third mechanic is identity and coding, and it is the one most likely to produce outright defaults. HaloMD reports that plans must register in the new IDR registry within 90 days, a window the same speakers later restate as 90 business days [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:15:34]. The penalty for skipping registration is severe. An unregistered plan cannot respond and defaults at the offer stage, and a plan that registers late is covered only for steps going forward [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:19:47]. KLGates adds that payers must use CARCs and RARCs to flag IDR eligibility and must include contact information with denials. That requirement is effective August 3, 2026 but still awaits further guidance from the agencies [NwapzBNojY0 @ 00:02:32]. The intake channel is changing at the same time. Xpert says the 30-day open-negotiation clock now runs from portal date stamps and that fax and email proof is 'completely dead.' Missing a stamp means permanently losing the dispute window, so the portal has to be monitored every day [CwSXrQBZiOg @ 00:03:36]. For payers, the registry is the sharpest edge in the rule, because missing registration converts a defensible dispute into a default at the offer stage. For providers, the remittance codes become the eligibility flag KLGates describes, telling billing teams which claims belong in the federal process.

callout.title: How the operators are actually running the new rulebook
callout.body: Billing shops, TPAs, and provider-side filers are converging on the same habits: separate the legacy and new-rule caseloads, document everything in writing, and police eligibility code by code before the portal or the arbitrator does it for you.
items: Split the caseload into pre- and post-November 1 tracking systems keyed on the open-negotiation start date, and run deadlines on a calendar-based tool rather than spreadsheets [Xpert Billing Talk — g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:01:47]

Radiology batching runs on Category I CPT codes. Coders must cross-reference manually, because mixing eligible and ineligible codes in one batch triggers automatic rejection [Xpert Billing Talk — g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:03:22]

Billing agencies initiate on everything and ignore negotiation requests, so log every good-faith outreach and submit the log in IDR, where it is considered, unlike settlement talks in litigation [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:03:31]

Anesthesia is usually elective, so it is IDR-eligible only if the facility was in-network. Check network status, admission type, and timelines on every claim and 'be the goalie' [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:06:46]

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest fight is over what Congress should bolt onto IDR. Tom Leefrieded of the AFL-CIO calls ranking member Pallone's bill "really the gold standard" because it trends 2019 rates forward, forces payment at 30 days, strips out ghost rates, mandates CMS audits of QPAs, and eliminates arbitration outright [9SCzxZp8uAE @ 00:34:14]. James Greenspan reads the same bill as a nonstarter. Pallone floated the identical idea in 2019, was overruled, and then signed the version that kept arbitration. The new bill has no co-sponsors and "not a lot of appetite on the Hill," so Greenspan treats it as an anchoring tactic ahead of next-Congress negotiations [HTDpgKwIfRg @ 00:00:33]. Brian O'Hara of The Phia Group sees a payer-side danger in a benchmark as well, warning that payers could end up setting rates unilaterally. O'Hara also points to New Jersey bills running $100K to $500K and assistant-surgeon claims topping $1M on a usual-and-customary basis that the NSA does not permit [8QIP4F1EGTA @ 00:17:27]. Greenspan flags a third lane that sidesteps the rate fight entirely: a possible Cassidy legacy bill. It would not narrow which cases qualify. Instead it would move the eligibility determination earlier in the process and make it binding, ending the repeated eligibility challenges that both sides now fight over on case after case [HTDpgKwIfRg @ 00:01:36].

Practitioners split just as hard on whether the system is broken or merely being abused. At the Coalition for Affordable Hospitals panel, Maya Holmes of the Culinary Health Fund rated the NSA net negative. Tom Leefrieded of the AFL-CIO rated it net positive, on the grounds that the patient protections are still needed [9SCzxZp8uAE @ 00:38:26]. Provider-side operators reject the runaway-cost story. Pilgrim of SCP Health says the group is now in network more often and at lower rates, and adds: "We are actually making less dollars after the No Surprises Act has been implemented than we did before" [PpfXacIXrAc @ 00:53:49]. Anders Gilberg of MGMA concedes that abuses exist but calls them "not the majority." Gilberg argues that payers are "hiding behind" egregious cases, such as a Florida physician's six-figure claim, when they should be offering amounts nearer to in-network rates [K4eVTdf3xa0 @ 00:08:37]. The payer camp answers with concentration data. Kenna Watts reports that five provider groups, four private-equity staffing groups plus HaloMD, file roughly three-quarters of all disputes. Watts adds that up to $1.4B has gone to contingency fees, and that staffing groups win 90% to 96% of the time with awards running 6 to 10 times median in-network rates [wJkWOgxZj6k @ 00:12:03].

The operations final rule itself gets graded on a curve. Gilberg, whose MGMA pushed for the cut in the initiation fee from $115 to $15, sums up the provider reaction: "we'll take it as a win and move on from there" [K4eVTdf3xa0 @ 00:16:02]. Katie Johnson of the American Benefits Council calls the same rules only an "initial step." They were proposed years ago, took a long time to finalize, and in the Council's view miss "the most egregious areas of abuse." The Council is pressing Congress and the Trump administration for more rigorous oversight [30BDiubQ0cg @ 00:00:59]. The litigation track divides operators too. Judge Kernodle sided with TMA on every QPA calculation point. Ron Howrigan of Fulcrum Strategies predicts that CMS still will not audit QPAs, so the next move is a "TMA-5" suit against CMS or a class action against carriers. Howrigan expects the class action to land harder [f9Q5ImwNeS0 @ 00:11:50]. Brady Bazar of The Phia Group runs the defensive play for TPAs. Plans should use a good-faith interpretation of the 2023 methodology until the Fifth Circuit rules en banc, document that approach without writing a "40page memo," and keep QPA disclosures carrying certification language [ksxW878eWWk @ 00:08:47].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The costliest firsthand trap is the clock. Xpert Billing Talk warns that batched disputes now sit through a new 30-business-day cooling-off period and then get a four-business-day filing window. The portal blocks late filings with no grace period, and those claims "just get dumped right into your denial management queues as permanent losses" [g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:02:36]. The HaloMD team hammers the same point on the batch resubmission window, which has been cut to 4 business days: "Do not miss this particular change because you will expire cases" [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:30:03]. The proof standard is tightening at the same time. The second Xpert Billing Talk breakdown says the 30-day open-negotiation clock now runs off portal date stamps and that fax and email proof is "completely dead." In that breakdown's words, "Missing a deadline now has zero margin for error," so the portal has to be monitored daily [CwSXrQBZiOg @ 00:03:54]. Xpert Billing Talk also says spreadsheets are not up to the job and teams need a calendar-based tracking tool. Radiology coders face an extra trap: they must manually cross-reference Category I CPT codes, because mixing eligible and ineligible codes in a batch triggers automatic rejection [g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:03:53].

Plans and TPAs report their own bleeding points. Brian O'Hara describes one claim split into 15 disputes, one per CPT code, spread across seven or eight IDREs with mixed outcomes: "Some IDREs have dismissed disputes, some are letting them go through, some we haven't heard back from" [8QIP4F1EGTA @ 00:07:06]. O'Hara also reports plans learning of determinations months after the fact. IDREs refuse to correct errors the provider caused, such as filing with the wrong email address, and eligibility problems surface in roughly half of all cases. O'Hara's verdict: "This is all the time" [8QIP4F1EGTA @ 00:16:00]. HaloMD flags a new default trap in the plan registry. A plan that has not registered cannot respond and defaults at the offer stage. Registering late helps only with steps going forward, because "It is forward-looking only" [of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:20:52]. Brady Bazar puts numbers on the eligibility war: eligibility was challenged in 40% of disputes, about 476,000 in the first half of 2025, making it the main bottleneck in the entire process. For TPAs, that turns eligibility proof into the core daily workload. The provider side faces the mirror image of that grind, since every one of those challenged filings is a claim stuck outside the payment pipeline [ksxW878eWWk @ 00:05:31].

Winning is not the same as collecting. Anders Gilberg says providers win more than 80% of the time but often go unpaid, which is why MGMA wants accountability for timely payment and why enforcement legislation is pending [K4eVTdf3xa0 @ 00:07:01]. Brady Bazar explains the hole. In Guardian Flight, the Fifth Circuit held there is no private right of action to enforce IDR awards, and the Supreme Court declined review, so enforcement runs through HHS civil penalties. Awards are still due within 30 calendar days, and nonpayment carries reputational and regulatory risk. TPAs are told to build an award-payment tracker [ksxW878eWWk @ 00:12:11]. On the payer ledger, Bartlett of ERIC describes one employer whose IDR costs went from $3.5M in 2025 to a $12M pace, about $4,000 in excess per claim, with settlements stretching from one month to three. Another employer is absorbing awards at 4.5 times billed charges [wJkWOgxZj6k @ 00:33:59]. The network fallout cuts both ways. Ron Howrigan cites an ASA survey in which more than 40% of respondents reported a UnitedHealthcare termination or threat of one, alongside Blue Cross NC threat letters. Both carriers stopped once the lawsuits began [f9Q5ImwNeS0 @ 00:19:50].

callout.title: Four Ways Disputes Die Before Anyone Argues the Merits
callout.body: Every item below is a loss practitioners watched happen on procedure alone, before an arbitrator ever weighed an offer.
items: Hard-calendar the four-business-day filing window after the 30-business-day cooling-off period, because the portal blocks late filings with no grace period and dumps them into denial queues as permanent losses [Xpert Billing Talk — g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:02:36].

Register every plan in the IDR registry before the deadline, because an unregistered plan cannot respond, defaults at the offer stage, and late registration only covers steps going forward [HaloMD — of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:19:47].
Verify the current administrative and entity fees before every payment, because paying the wrong fee means your offer is denied [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:17:28].

Run an award-payment tracker against the 30-calendar-day deadline, because unpaid awards carry reputational and regulatory risk even without a private right of action [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:14:13].

chapters.pull_quote: "Do not miss this particular change because you will expire cases." attributed to HaloMD (of6CD7esHY0 @ 00:30:03).
action_checklist: Split the dispute caseload into pre- and post-November 1, 2026 tracking systems keyed on the open-negotiation start date [Xpert Billing Talk — g3C-DoM_9CI @ 00:01:47].
Log every good-faith negotiation outreach and submit the log in IDR, because it is considered there, unlike settlement talks in litigation [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:03:31].
Audit workflows now, build in the new CARC/RARC codes, and revisit low-dollar claims under the lower administrative fee [KLGatesLaw — NwapzBNojY0 @ 00:06:25].
As the non-initiating party, issue a response by the 15th business day of the 30-business-day open negotiation period [KLGatesLaw — NwapzBNojY0 @ 00:04:19].
Build a dispute dashboard that flags repeat initiators, and back eligibility challenges with EOBs and internal network records kept clear and concise [The Phia Group, LLC — ksxW878eWWk @ 00:15:55].

chapters.question_prompt: What does the CMS public use file data show about IDR volume, win rates, and award levels, and how are those outcomes affecting employer plans and premiums?
chapters.title: Reading the IDR Scoreboard: Volume, Win Rates, Award Levels, and the Premium Fallout
chapters.subtitle: 2024 CMS public use file trends, provider win rates and awards vs. QPA, financial viability of IDR for radiology, the $15 billion arbitration year, employer-sponsored plan cost impact, the 2027 premium spike argument, IDR-driven consolidation, and competing myth-vs-reality data narratives
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners across employer, payer-analytics, policy and provider-filer camps read the same IDR scoreboard. Volume blew far past the 17,000-22,000 annual cases regulators expected, reaching 1.4M disputes in 2024 and 2.2M-2.6M in 2025, and one anesthesia operator cites a 5M run rate. Providers win roughly 80-90% of baseball-style decisions. Awards cluster around 4-4.5x QPA, and in one Texas pool they spiked to 25x the in-network average for assistant surgeons and 65x for path/lab. A handful of filers (Radiology Partners, TeamHealth, SCP, HaloMD) drive half or more of volume. Employers report broken budgets, stop-loss exposure and premium pressure. HaloMD counters that only 6.1% of eligible claims reach IDR, that insurers defaulted on 24% of their losses, and that QPA itself is set too low. The admin fee has now dropped to $15, and operators expect another filing surge.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus — Volume Exploded, Providers Win, Employers Pay
paragraphs: Every camp reading the scoreboard agrees on the first line: volume exploded. Regulators planned for roughly 17,000 to 22,000 disputes a year. Chris Keyser of the Texas Business Group on Health counts more than 7 million cases opened since 2022, adding about $22B to the system [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:05:50]. Zelis counts 1.4M disputes in 2024, up 115%. More than 600,000 were still pending going into 2025, and 69% of open disputes were older than 30 days. Its blunt verdict is that the system is broken [lhoUoQSpOCg @ 00:00:23]. The Atlantic reporting narrated by Long Reads, Explained puts 2025 at 2.6 million provider-filed disputes. Providers trigger more than 99% of them, and first-half 2026 volume is running another 50% higher [cSaC2n-3r9o @ 00:06:58]. Dr. Eric Bricker tracks the quarterly climb from 200,000 to 250,000 to over 300,000 disputes. He frames the original problem plainly: out-of-network radiology, ER, anesthesiology, pathology and surgical-assistant groups were billing patients who had walked into in-network hospitals [6E_HRECi-t8 @ 00:02:04]. The volume figures disagree at the edges, and every speaker reports the curve still climbing. Operators should treat dispute count as a rising baseline rather than a one-time spike that will fade on its own.

The second line of consensus is the win rate. IDR is baseball-style arbitration. Each side submits one best offer, and the arbitrator picks one without splitting the difference. Under that format, Bricker reports physician groups winning 80 to 85% of the time. Carriers offer the QPA, the median in-network rate, while providers average about 4.5x QPA. Radiology lands near 6x QPA and neurosurgery at 11x QPA, roughly 16x Medicare [6E_HRECi-t8 @ 00:02:19]. Dr. Tia Sawhney is an FSA and NYU adjunct who previously worked prepayment recovery. She puts the provider win rate above 85% and calls the system statistically biased toward providers. Offers are not disclosed, and there is no rebuttal and no appeal [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:11:42]. The anesthesia-side operator at About The Rest says sophisticated groups running baseball-style arbitration win 85 to 88% [x35n4T9CppE @ 00:01:03]. HaloMD's Becker's panel cites the latest CMS report at 86%, up from 84% [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:07:21]. Bricker's sharpest single example is a surgical assistant awarded $200,000 for one operation, which left that employer running over budget. The read for any plan operator is that once the counterparty files, the base case is a loss at a multiple of the plan's own benchmark rather than a negotiated middle.

The third consensus point is that a small number of filers run the scoreboard and employers absorb the bill. Sawhney counts 2.2M disputes in 2025, with about half coming from five vendors. HaloMD alone filed more than 400,000 and is paid a percentage of the uplift [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:09:31]. The Atlantic reporting assigns half of filings to Radiology Partners and TeamHealth combined and 27% to HaloMD. It names IDR the largest single driver of next year's premium increase, at 25 to 40%, ahead of GLP-1s and AI coding. National IDR cost ran $1.6B a year from 2022 through 2024 and hit $16.6B in 2025 [cSaC2n-3r9o @ 00:15:45]. Texas employers put the damage in budget terms. The Texas Health Benefits Pool spent more than $20M in added claims and fees, and the panel states that self-funded employers bear about 90% of IDR costs [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:51:59]. Loren Adler of Brookings confirms the pass-through. These awards do not just come out of insurer margins; they flow into premiums and cost-sharing, with the hit showing in 2026 and more in 2027 [c7whA-tTpq4 @ 00:04:30]. For an employer or plan operator, the consensus is that IDR is now a recurring premium line item rather than a rounding error buried in claims.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers — Ticket Cost, Filing Engines, Payer Countermoves
paragraphs: The street math starts with the cost of a ticket. Eric Christensen of the Neiman Health Policy Institute lays out the fee ladder. The administrative fee was $50 in 2022 and $350 in 2023, until a court vacated it back to $50, and then $115 in 2024. On top of that sits a loser-pays entity fee that climbed from $200-$500 to $200-$1,173, which puts the expected cost to enter IDR at $173 to $455 [rYqWvbw_kGo @ 00:02:41]. Under the 2023 batching rules, claims could ride together if they shared billing code and modifiers, health plan and a 30-business-day window. Even so, the average batch held only 3.1 claims, or 2.2 for radiology. His viability math is brutal for small tickets. Recovering a quarter of the charge-minus-QPA gap makes IDR worth it on only 35 to 52% of claims overall and 11 to 22% of radiology claims [rYqWvbw_kGo @ 00:04:54]. The ticket price has since collapsed. HaloMD confirms the $15 admin fee is already in effect, alongside a 50-line batch cap from November 1 and a cooling-off period cut to 30 business days [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:49:59]. The About The Rest operator reads the drop from $115 to $15 bluntly: now you are going to have a tidal wave of new filings [x35n4T9CppE @ 00:01:40].

The filer side runs IDR as a production line, and HaloMD's leadership walks through the engine. Alla Laro ranks win ratio only about fifth when choosing an IDR entity. Refund speed matters most: entities have 30 business days to refund, and the good ones do it in 5. Next come eligibility accuracy, flexible batching and award timeliness, and 4 entities routinely beat the 30-business-day award deadline [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:28:04]. Megan Roush's back-office rule is equally mechanical: enroll in ACH refunds with all 11 IDR entities and expect some of them to demand verbal bank authentication before money moves [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:21:09]. Nutex Health shows the payoff curve. Revenue across its 24 hospitals in 11 states fell 35% when the NSA started. Nutex began IDR in Q2/Q3 2024 with 60 to 70% of visits eligible and an 80 to 90% win rate. Results took 4 to 5 months to arrive, and revenue then rose 270% year over year [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:38:19]. HaloMD's data session adds the payer-side weakness the engine leans on. 24% of insurer losses were outright defaults, where the insurer submitted no offer at all and could not have been named the prevailing party, and 8.2% involved insurer offers of $1 or less [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:30:43].

On the payer and employer side, the mechanics start with finding the disputes at all. Sawhney's detection tell is a claim payment reversed two to six months later and then repaid at a much higher amount. Reason codes exist, but they are often not shared with the employer [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:39:40]. Bricker tells employers to demand their claims with IDR claims flagged and to expect a we-can't-or-we-won't answer. In his view, not knowing which claims went through IDR is almost de facto not being an adequate fiduciary [6E_HRECi-t8 @ 00:07:36]. The Texas Health Benefits Pool's Jennifer Hoff measured awards against the in-network average: 5x for ER facility, 10x for ER physician, 16x for anesthesia, 25x for assistant surgeon, 30x for neuromonitoring and 65x for path and lab. The pool countered with Green Imaging, Tap telehealth putting an ER physician on screen within 2 minutes, DPC, and opting into the state IDR [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:19:34]. San Antonio's Renee Freda tracked freestanding ER visits costing 138% more, rising from $732 to $1,742. She found informal settlements landing at 200 to 240% of Medicare versus roughly 400% through IDR, a spread that makes direct settlement the cheaper exit whenever a filer will take the call [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:32:15].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The loudest split is over whether the dispute flood is abuse or arithmetic. The narration of Roge Karma's Atlantic piece sets the critic baseline: regulators budgeted for 17,000 disputes a year, providers filed 2.6 million in 2025, providers trigger more than 99% of them, and first-half 2026 volume is running up 50% [cSaC2n-3r9o @ 00:06:58]. The anesthesia-side operator at About The Rest goes further, calling the real run rate 5 million against the 17,000 prediction, and reads the fee drop from $115 to $15 as the trigger for a tidal wave of new filings [x35n4T9CppE @ 00:01:40]. HaloMD's Patrick attacks the premise itself: the 17,000 estimate was built on New York data that excluded emergency medicine, and re-running the projection on Texas data produces 1.54 million disputes in year one and 2.69 million by year four, against roughly 2.5 million actually filed [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:09:18]. The same HaloMD deck argues the system is under-used rather than abused, because only 6.1% of 19.7 million eligible claims ever reach arbitration [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:12:15]. Volume figures quoted across these speakers range from 1.4 million to 5 million disputes, so the number that lands on a board slide depends entirely on whose count is used, which year is measured, and whether the speaker is filing disputes or paying the resulting awards.

The second fault line is who is gaming whom. Provider-side figures quoted in the Atlantic narration say 8% of insurer offers were $1 or less and 25% of disputes drew no counteroffer at all, while Hoadley counters that 90% of insurer offers sit at or above the QPA and that HCSC alone staffs more than 400 people on IDR [cSaC2n-3r9o @ 00:11:39]. HaloMD presses the provider case with public-use-file math: 24% of insurer losses were defaults where the payer submitted no offer at all and could not have been named the prevailing party, and 8.2% involved offers of $1 or less [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:30:43]. Chris Keyser, speaking to Texas employers, estimates that about 40% of disputes should never have been filed, yet refuses to pick a side, blaming plans for low offers and providers for flooding the system with roughly 15 entities paid only when a case is filed [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:10:12]. Eligibility is the sharpest numeric clash: non-initiating parties claimed 42% of disputes were ineligible, but the arbitration entities themselves found only 19% ineligible [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:17:20]. The street read for payers is blunt: skipping the offer step is a free win handed to the filer, and for providers, junk filings feed the 40% narrative that employers and their lobbyists now carry into every hearing.

The third disagreement is whether the benchmark or the award is the broken number. Dr. Tia Sawhney says pricing fails at both ends: the QPA is too low because it is a 2019 median trended by CPI-U, padded with ghost rates and weighting providers equally, yet awards land at 10 to 100 times market value [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:08:45]. HaloMD argues only the first half, citing the TMA3 ruling that found the QPA methodology unlawful, claiming that stripping ghost rates can lift the in-network figure up to 600%, and quoting NDP work showing 60% of QPAs mismatched with the true median about 290% higher [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:33:10]. The same HaloMD team claims roughly $3 billion in emergency-medicine savings versus pre-NSA, a direct collision with the Texas Health Benefits Pool, which reports more than $20 million in added claims and fees and says half of a 16.5% three-year rate rise traces to the NSA [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:14:40]. On fixes, Loren Adler of Brookings prefers a hard benchmark such as 250% of Medicare or an in-network guarantee that matches networks, while HaloMD urges its audience to back the Murphy bill and critics point to a House proposal that would scrap IDR outright [c7whA-tTpq4 @ 00:12:00].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is filing claims that cannot pay for themselves. Eric Christensen of the Neiman Health Policy Institute puts the expected cost to enter IDR at $173 to $455 once the administrative fee and the loser-pays entity fee are blended, with entity fees climbing as high as $1,173 in 2024 [rYqWvbw_kGo @ 00:02:41]. At a realistic recovery of one quarter of the charge-minus-QPA gap, IDR pencils out for only 11% to 22% of radiology claims, leaving three-quarters to nine-tenths of radiology claims underwater, and the average radiology batch held just 2.2 claims under the 2023 batching rules [rYqWvbw_kGo @ 00:04:54]. HaloMD's Alla Laro confirms the pain from the filer side, flagging the fee burden that radiology's small claims carry into every dispute [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:17:45]. Then the economics flipped: the About The Rest operator reports the fee falling from $115 to $15 and predicts that groups running an IDR engine will thrive while everyone else gets screwed [x35n4T9CppE @ 00:01:40]. The pre-filing check is plain arithmetic on fee exposure against a quarter-share of the delta, and Christensen adds a structural warning on top: because the QPA sits below in-network rates, clinicians lose bargaining leverage, so a lost dispute costs more than the entity fee alone.

The second trap is winning on paper and never getting paid. Laro says about 70% of disputes are paid late even though payment is due within 30 calendar days, and that payers raise objections after awards despite a 3-day statutory objection window and award finality [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:16:53]. Megan Roush traces 95% of payment failures to missing data such as the EOB and award letter, tells filers to send that packet proactively, net out recoup-and-repay remittances, and stop trusting CARC and RARC codes [g2udecJ21bI @ 00:23:45]. HaloMD's employer-facing webinar claims one in four or more awards are withheld, pushes employers to grill their TPAs with uncomfortable questions, and flags anecdotal shared-savings fees charged on the award delta [oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:44:51]. Enforcement is thin on every side of the table. Loren Adler notes there is no clear private right of action, courts are split, and the government can fine insurers but has not done so [c7whA-tTpq4 @ 00:08:12]. The Crowell litigator at the Texas webinar adds that courts have dismissed nearly all IDR process cases, which matches the About The Rest report that payers suing everyone have lost or been dismissed. An award is a receivable, and the collection workflow decides realized yield.

The third set of failures lands on self-funded plans. The Texas Health Benefits Pool pushed 9,000-plus claims through review, found 370 ineligible worth about $200,000, and could not appeal any of them [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:17:00]. The City of San Antonio watched IDR claims climb from $18 million in FY25 to a projected $43 million in FY26, with fees jumping from $1.4 million to $10.5 million, until 24% of medical claims spend went to IDR [8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:28:17]. Sawhney's elective-surgery warning is the nastiest leak: an unsigned consent form lets a physician file, assistant surgeons, anesthesiologists, and neuromonitoring providers are interlinked, and a $20,000 to $40,000 surgery can turn into $500,000 to $800,000 [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:20:47]. Detection is the bottleneck because reason codes exist but are often not shared; the tell Sawhney teaches is a payment reversed two to six months later and repaid much higher [lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:39:40]. Jennifer Hoff adds that plans with lower stop-loss attachment points are the exposed ones, and Sawhney notes there is no appeal, with the only recourse a CMS web gripe. Plans that cannot see these claims, in Dr. Eric Bricker's words, are almost de facto not adequate fiduciaries.

callout.title: Four Checks Before Filing or Paying Another IDR Dispute
callout.body: Each check below comes straight from a practitioner who lost money, lost time, or lost a dispute on the point. Run all four before the next batch goes out or the next award gets paid.
items: Verify benefits before filing, because 20 states run bifurcated state and NSA rules, deadlines fall at 3, 4, and 10 days, and open-negotiation notices sent to wrong addresses such as MultiPlan or Zelis sink disputes [HaloMD — g2udecJ21bI @ 00:44:00].

Enroll in ACH refunds with all 11 IDR entities, including those that require verbal bank authentication, and request custom reports weekly from the 6 entities that offer them [HaloMD — g2udecJ21bI @ 00:21:09].
Price every claim against the fee load first, since a one-quarter recovery of the charge-minus-QPA gap leaves only 11% to 22% of radiology claims viable [AJR Radiology — rYqWvbw_kGo @ 00:04:54].

On the plan side, demand claims data with IDR claims flagged and expect the carrier to say it can't or won't, because not knowing which claims went through IDR is almost de facto inadequate fiduciary conduct [AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained — 6E_HRECi-t8 @ 00:07:50].

chapters.pull_quote: "Today, 24% of our medical claims spend is just on IDR." — Renee Freda, City of San Antonio, attributed to Texas Business group on Health (8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:28:17).
action_checklist: Demand your claims file from the carrier with every IDR claim flagged, and document the refusal when the answer is that they can't or won't (AHealthcareZ - Healthcare Finance Explained, 6E_HRECi-t8 @ 00:07:36).
Scan payment history for claims paid, reversed two to six months later, and repaid at a much higher amount, since IDR reason codes are often withheld (Payerset, lqE3aZxq024 @ 00:39:40).
Put your TPA through a set of uncomfortable questions on withheld awards and shared-savings fees charged on the delta (HaloMD, oEWBNDsvXOQ @ 00:44:51).

Select IDR entities on refund speed, eligibility accuracy, batching flexibility, and timeliness first, ranking win ratio around fifth, and lock agreement before midnight to avoid the random pool (HaloMD, g2udecJ21bI @ 00:28:04).
Send the EOB and award letter to the payer proactively on every win, since 95% of payment failures trace to missing data (HaloMD, g2udecJ21bI @ 00:23:45).
Steer members to Green Imaging, Tap telehealth, and DPC, and opt into the state IDR where available, to shrink exposure at the source (Texas Business group on Health, 8zjJbZyS2j8 @ 00:20:25).

chapters.question_prompt: Once a provider wins in IDR, how do they actually collect—and which specialties are fighting the hardest IDR battles?
chapters.title: Winning vs. Getting Paid: Unpaid Awards and the Specialty IDR Battlegrounds
chapters.subtitle: Insurers' roughly 30% unpaid awards, enforcement pushes, award collection services, IONM revenue strategy and the 'paid too much' critique, anesthesia IDR economics, emergency medicine legal risk and physician leverage, and air ambulance operations
chapters.executive_summary: Winning an IDR award and collecting it are two separate fights. Practitioners agree providers win most disputes. Ed Gaines puts plan losses at 85-90% at 6-8x Medicare. Yet HaloMD's analysis of 400,000 awards found about 30% unpaid, with Anthem at 74% and rising to 83%, and Patrick Velicky pegs nonpayment near 35%. There is no private right of action, and the $100/day fine has never been issued. So the collection playbook runs through AR follow-up with the signed award letter, bulk department-of-insurance complaints, contingency recovery shops charging 8% of the amount recovered, and lobbying for the No Surprises Act Enforcement Act. Anesthesia, IONM, emergency medicine and air ambulance carry the heaviest award fights. The main disagreement is over volume strategy. The About The Rest panel warns that filing IDR on 100% of claims, at $1,000 per dispute with 9-12 month payment lags, can sink vendors within about 18 months.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus - The Award Letter Is Not Cash
paragraphs: Every collector, billing firm and IDR shop agrees on the core point: the award letter is not cash. HaloMD handed The Times an analysis of 400,000 arbitration awards. It showed roughly 30% unpaid since 2024, with Anthem's unpaid rate at 74% and climbing to 83% this year. Cigna disputed the figures, and the sample covers about two-thirds of HaloMD wins [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:04:46]. Patrick Velicky of HaloMD runs a shop that handles about 22% of all IDR initiations and serves mostly small independent groups. He puts nonpayment at about 35% and says some clients have waited more than a year for money they already won [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:17:28]. CollectionPro Services frames the same gap commercially. Payment is generally due within 30 calendar days of the determination, yet some winners go unpaid for months or years. The firm pitches pursuit of eligible awards that have sat unpaid for nearly two years [Ahr00pn-Tiw @ 00:00:00]. The insurer counter-story runs alongside the numbers. Elevance's Bayewitz argues most claims should have been ineligible, and Anthem says 60% of its cases were ineligible. On double awards, HCSC's Goldberg says, 'We're not going to pay it twice' [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:16:25]. From day one, operators should model award value and collected value as two separate revenue lines.

Practitioners also agree that the enforcement backstop is close to empty. Three appeals courts have held there is no private right to sue. The $100-per-day fine has never been issued: 'So far, it has not issued a single penalty' [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:12:00]. Laura Trotter of Apex IONM Solutions describes payers now asking providers outright, 'What are you going to do if I don't pay?' Her answer is uncomfortable. The available recourse is an AR process and sending the IDR-signed award letter. If funds are still not released, there is 'no recourse,' because most suits have been dismissed over unclear congressional intent [gbhlBlDLViQ @ 00:02:00]. Complaints to CMS do not fix it either. Trotter reports the agency is understaffed and flooded, the standard reply is 'we will assign an investigator,' and following up 'is not going to go anywhere' [gbhlBlDLViQ @ 00:04:22]. Ed Gaines of Zotec Partners traces the root cause to scale. The projection was about 17,000 disputes, providers filed more than 2.5 million across 2024 and 2025, and the whole process ended up under resourced [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:37:48]. The shared conclusion is that the provider side has to manufacture collection pressure entirely on its own, because neither the agencies nor the courts are supplying it.

Practitioners also agree on who is winning on the merits and where the fights concentrate. Gaines says plans lose 85-90% of cases, at awards of 6-8x Medicare, and builds that into the leverage story for independent physicians [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:38:48]. On the About The Rest panel, mediators are reported siding with anesthesia 85-90% of the time, with some awards reaching 7-12x Medicare. The panel credits IDR with balancing payers that were pushing rates down or pushing groups out of network [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:19:03]. Trotter explains why IONM wins so often. The same SSEP/EMG codes cover a 15-minute clinic test and hours of multimodal intraoperative monitoring near the CNS, so IDR entities agree with IONM providers 'more often than not' [EE3aFeVfLnk @ 00:00:57]. Air ambulance and emergency groups are where unpaid balances turn existential. Anthem owes Flight for Life $2.1 million, on flights ranging from $9,382 to $62,373. Wake Emergency won 1,032 cases but has $1.2 million outstanding and needed a credit line for payroll. PHI closed its Red Bluff base, citing $16.3 million owed by Anthem [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:14:17]. Winning on volume without collecting simply converts operating profit into aging receivables that payroll cannot spend.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers - From Filing to Funds
paragraphs: The baseline mechanics are simple and unforgiving. Each side submits a single dollar figure, and the arbitrator picks one with no splitting. The insurer is then supposed to pay within 30 days, and balance billing the patient stays prohibited [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:02:32]. Attorney Andrew Bethel lays out the front end. There is a 30-business-day open negotiation period. Multiple items, such as anesthesiology plus radiology, can be batched into one dispute. Notice goes to the federal portal the same day it goes to the other party. He also warns that only 39% of submitted disputes had been resolved, leaving roughly 300,000 open [q3heX6QnFfo @ 00:04:42]. Gaines prices the administrative fee at $115 per dispute [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:38:30]. The About The Rest panel adds the real cost: 'you might get $50 a unit as a QPA initially, but then you have to spend $1,000 per dispute to the IDRE.' Payment takes 9-12 months. Some companies win only 50-60% and lose money. Only about half of states use the federal process. The average award lands around 2.3x QPA, or ask 150, get 100 [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:20:29]. Every won dispute therefore carries a filing fee, a months-long lag and a collection risk before it ever becomes cash.

The pricing fight is where the multiples get won. Gaines teaches the sharpest tactic: pull transparency allowed-amount data by plan, zip, CPT and TIN to argue market rates. His example is 250% of Medicare in the market versus the 120% a plan actually paid. 'I can look up any TIN in the country and know exactly what they're getting paid,' he says [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:41:15]. Velicky attacks the benchmark itself. The QPA rests on 2019 rates plus inflation, TMA 3 found the QPA calculation unlawful, and Avalere work with ASA identified 'ghost rates' [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:08:55]. The Apex Revenue Fix host reports payers setting the QPA as a Medicare multiplier, 'sometimes as low as like 80% of Medicare rates.' Spine, brain and vascular cases can arbitrate to about $17,000 or more. Claims get priced at the average in-network amount, and demanding more forces negotiation or arbitration [QRrun6dHMIY @ 00:07:32]. Trotter's IONM argument closes the loop. The QPA is the median contracted rate per billing code, and identical SSEP/EMG codes cover both a 15-minute clinic test and hours of intraoperative monitoring. That is why IDR entities side with IONM providers 'more often than not' [EE3aFeVfLnk @ 00:00:37]. Running that playbook with clean coding, Apex reports it has 'doubled, tripled, and quadrupled revenue' for many clients.

Once an award is won, the collection stack is manual and escalating. Trotter's sequence starts with a standard AR process and sending the IDR-signed award letter. It then moves to bulk complaints filed with the departments of insurance, which she treats as pre-litigation. She adds that payments trend toward release when insurers lose lawsuits [gbhlBlDLViQ @ 00:05:45]. CollectionPro Services productizes the back end. It reviews unpaid awards, pursues payers, escalates compliance issues and coordinates legal intervention, and it says it can chase eligible awards unpaid for nearly two years. It targets payments credited within 30-60 days as 'a focused effort to get you paid.' The fee is 8% of the amount recovered, payable only after funds hit the provider's account: 'No recovery, no success fee' [Ahr00pn-Tiw @ 00:01:16]. Velicky points to a pressure point inside employer plans. TPAs charge fees on out-of-network claims, and Elevance disclosed to employers that it withholds award payments, which creates ERISA exposure. In his shared-savings example, the insurer takes 40% of the $900 delta on a $1,000 bill with $100 allowed [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:13:07]. On the patient side, Fine Print Files routes unresolved surprise bills to 1-800-985-3059 or the state Department of Insurance. Insurers are asked to reprocess claims, and every date, time and name gets logged [qo0CHDEWdi4 @ 00:07:19].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is whether IDR is a growth engine or a slow-burning liability. Laura Trotter of Apex IONM Solutions opens bluntly with "I like out of network" and claims arbitration workflows, clean coding, and denial counteraction have "doubled, tripled, and quadrupled revenue" for clients [QRrun6dHMIY @ 00:03:02]. About The Rest pushes back hard: host Joe Rodriguez warns payment lands 9 to 12 months out, each dispute costs $1,000, and some companies winning only 50 to 60 percent lose money outright [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:20:29]. Randy of North Star goes further, describing vendors who win hospital bids on IDR revenue assumptions, plan to IDR 100 percent of their claims, and hit business trouble in roughly 18 months because "at some point in time, the music's gonna stop" [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:23:46]. Randy's alternative is to treat IDR as a threat rather than a volume business, since the credible threat of filing is itself leverage at the negotiating table [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:26:55]. Patrick Velicky of HaloMD, whose firm handles about 22 percent of IDR initiations and serves mostly small independent groups, lands in the middle: anesthesia practices should use IDR to move toward sustainable in-network contracts and treat it as a hedge against consolidation in their markets [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:26:22].

Practitioners also disagree on how big the nonpayment hole is and who is to blame. HaloMD's analysis of 400,000 awards, reported by Long Reads, Explained, puts about 30 percent unpaid since 2024, with Anthem at 74 percent and rising to 83 percent this year, though the sample covers only trackable payments and Cigna disputed the figures [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:04:46]. Callagy Law's number is 27 percent still unpaid six months after decision, while Velicky pegs nonpayment at about 35 percent [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:17:28]. The insurer playbook flips the frame: Elevance's Bayewitz says most claims should have been ineligible, Anthem says 60 percent of its cases were ineligible, and HCSC's Goldberg refuses double awards with "We're not going to pay it twice" [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:16:25]. On recovery routes, Laura Trotter writes off CMS follow-up as something that "is not going to go anywhere" and instead pushes bulk complaints to state departments of insurance as pre-litigation, noting payments trend toward release when insurers lose lawsuits [gbhlBlDLViQ @ 00:05:45]. CollectionPro Services LLC sells the outsourced alternative: review unpaid awards, pursue payers, escalate compliance issues, coordinate legal intervention, and take 8 percent only after money actually lands in the provider's account [Ahr00pn-Tiw @ 00:01:16].

The specialty battlegrounds split along benchmark lines. In emergency medicine, John Bedolla of The Center for Medical Education treated federal median-rate bills as an "existential threat" that lets carriers terminate contracts and cut pay "50% or at least 30%" [uqsbhH3wss0 @ 00:57:43]. Ed Gaines of Zotec tells the opposite outcome story: the Ways and Means IDR version beat the Energy and Commerce bill that had no IDR, the Texas Medical Association won four lawsuits against QPA-favoring rules, and plans now lose 85 to 90 percent of cases at 6 to 8 times Medicare [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:38:48]. Gaines holds up California's AB 72, benchmarked at 125 percent of Medicare, as the cautionary alternative where incomes fell and recruiting lost ground to Texas. In neuromonitoring, Laura Trotter rejects the insurer story that IONM wins too much, arguing the same SSEP and EMG codes cover a 15-minute clinic test and hours of intraoperative monitoring, so IDR entities side with IONM "more often than not" [EE3aFeVfLnk @ 00:01:34]. In anesthesia, Dr. Brian Schmutzer reports mediators siding with anesthesia 85 to 90 percent of the time, with some awards at 7 to 12 times Medicare, framed as a counterweight to payers pushing rates down or pushing groups out of network [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:19:03].

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first trap is assuming a win equals cash. Long Reads, Explained reports three appeals courts holding there is no private right to sue, and the $100-a-day nonpayment fine has never been issued: "So far, it has not issued a single penalty" [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:12:00]. Laura Trotter of Apex IONM Solutions describes payers openly asking providers "What are you going to do if I don't pay?" and says once the IDR-signed award letter goes out through AR and funds still are not released, there is "no recourse" [gbhlBlDLViQ @ 00:01:18]. CMS complaints hit an understaffed, "flooded" agency whose standard reply is that an investigator will be assigned. The damage is concrete. Wake Emergency won 1,032 cases, still had $1.2 million outstanding, and needed a credit line to make payroll [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:13:30]. PHI closed its Red Bluff base citing $16.3 million owed by Anthem, while Anthem countered that PHI asks $56,000 per flight. Flight for Life is owed $2.1 million by Anthem after payments "suddenly stopped." Velicky reports some HaloMD clients waiting more than a year to be paid, and says Elevance disclosed to employers that it withholds award payments, creating ERISA exposure for the insurer [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:18:15].

The second trap is unit economics that only work on paper. Joe Rodriguez of About The Rest lays out the math: "You might get $50 a unit as a QPA initially, but then you have to spend $1,000 per dispute to the IDRE," and the average award comes out around 2.3 times QPA, meaning you ask 150 and get 100 [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:20:44]. Rodriguez adds that only about half of states use the federal process at all. Ed Gaines frames the fee side differently, citing a $115 administrative fee per dispute and a system built for 17,000 projected disputes that drew more than 2.5 million in 2024 and 2025, leaving the whole process under-resourced [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:38:30]. Velicky's loss data shows how insurers bleed on their own side of the ledger: 24 percent of insurer losses are no-shows and 9.5 percent involve offers of $1 or less [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:21:38], while IDR itself takes at least 60 to 90 days [0BcGdvWG_UI @ 00:25:18]. Attorney Andrew Bethel adds the backlog reality: only 39 percent of submitted disputes resolved, leaving roughly 300,000 open, "so not a fast process by any stretch of the imagination" [q3heX6QnFfo @ 00:05:17].

The third trap is payer retaliation and eligibility blowback. Randy of North Star reports payers cancelling or threatening facility contracts, and one payer telling hospitals that vendors using IDR are "done"; Indiana banned that tactic in its 2026 session, while a separate 10 percent claim penalty was struck down [WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:24:32]. Ed Gaines flags Anthem's policy effective January 1, 2026, cutting facility rates 10 percent per non-par group with ED exempt, which Gaines calls a per se illegal boycott and tortious interference; Anthem is also suing 11 Prime hospitals over $15 million in alleged fraudulent awards [QITUqT322Iw @ 00:46:25]. Eligibility is the insurer counterpunch: filing deadlines, Medicare and Medicaid exclusions, and contracted-provider exclusions knock claims out, arbitrators earn their flat fee only on eligible rulings, and five insurers sued HaloMD, though three suits were dismissed [nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:16:47]. For startups, Laura Trotter warns insurance credentialing takes a few months and differs from hospital credentialing, and arbitration adds more months on top, so founders should subcontract while credentialing, hold a per-case rate covering overhead for the first few months, and keep side income while scaling [QRrun6dHMIY @ 00:10:17].

callout.title: Four Checks Before You Scale IDR Filings
callout.body: Every item below comes from a loss, stall, or reversal practitioners hit firsthand. Clear all four before treating IDR wins as revenue.
items: Do not book an award as cash until it lands: about 30 percent of HaloMD's 400,000 awards were unpaid, with Anthem at 74 percent [Long Reads, Explained — nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:04:46].
Price every dispute before filing: a $50 unit QPA against $1,000 per dispute means a 50 to 60 percent win rate loses money [About The Rest — WdSfoeegaaI @ 00:20:44].
Screen eligibility up front: deadlines, Medicare and Medicaid exclusions, and contracted providers are the grounds insurers use to refuse payment [Long Reads, Explained — nJ5Tz7G_LA8 @ 00:08:37].
Fund the runway: credentialing takes a few months and arbitration adds more, so keep side income and plan to scale [Apex IONM Solutions — QRrun6dHMIY @ 00:10:17].
